claims.text: QUIC multiplexes independent streams that are retransmitted separately when lost, preventing head-of-line blocking. At 1% packet loss, QUIC maintains page load times within 5% of the loss-free baseline, while HTTP/2 degrades 30%+. Under extreme conditions (4% loss and 50ms latency), QUIC completes 10 MB downloads in 15 seconds versus HTTP/2's 106 seconds—a 7× speedup—because QUIC continues transmitting unaffected streams while resending only the lost stream, whereas TCP stalls all pending data until the missing packet arrives.

claims.text: QUIC's per-stream retransmission queues maintain throughput as packet loss increases, while TCP's single-connection queue stalls. At 2% packet loss, QUIC delivers 820 Mbps aggregate throughput compared to TCP's 380 Mbps—a 2.16× advantage. This occurs because TCP's single retransmission queue starves the entire pipeline until the missing packet arrives, whereas QUIC resends only affected streams and continues filling the connection window with others.

claims.text: QUIC's poor performance on high-bandwidth networks stems from receiver-side processing overhead, not transmission capacity limits. Two root causes are (1) lack of UDP generic receive offload (GRO), causing the kernel to issue significantly more packet reads via netif_receive_skb than TCP does, and (2) user-space ACK generation without delayed-ACK optimization. CPU frequency directly limits QUIC throughput: reducing it from 3.4 GHz to 1.6 GHz drops QUIC to 200 Mbps while HTTP/2 sustains above 900 Mbps.

claims.text: HTTP/3's performance advantage over HTTP/2 emerges around 2-4% packet loss and grows monotonically beyond. At 2-4% loss alone, both protocols perform similarly, but when combined with realistic 50ms mobile latency, the divergence becomes severe: at 4% loss and 50ms delay, HTTP/3 downloads complete in 15 seconds while HTTP/2 requires 106 seconds—a 7-fold penalty. This advantage continues at higher loss rates; at 12% loss, HTTP/3 achieves 81.5% improvement. Since typical mobile networks operate in the 2-5% loss range, HTTP/3 is the baseline requirement, not an exception.

claims.text: HTTP/3's mobile advantage is compounded by seamless connection migration across network transitions (Wi-Fi to cellular). During handoffs, HTTP/3 maintains an 88.36% latency advantage at 4% loss and 50ms delay—independent of packet loss rate itself. This migration advantage applies whenever IP addresses change, a routine occurrence for mobile devices. Combined with the observed loss-based advantage that persists across all tested loss rates, operators can segment HTTP/3 rollout by handoff frequency and device mobility patterns rather than by static baseline loss.
